title: State Management — Combine & Observation
summary: ObservableObject and @Published pushing state to views, Combine's operator pipelines, and the newer Observation framework that replaces most of the boilerplate.

slides.markdown:
`@State` in [SwiftUI Fundamentals](swiftui-fundamentals) covers state owned by a single view. Real apps need state that outlives any one view — a logged-in user, a shopping cart, a view model driving a whole screen's worth of data from the network.

That's the job of **ObservableObject** and **Combine**: a reference type that publishes changes, and views that subscribe and re-render when it does. This topic covers that machinery, Combine's pipeline operators for shaping async data, and the newer **Observation** framework that quietly fixes most of the reasons ObservableObject earned a reputation for over-firing updates.

slides.subTitle: pushing state changes to views

slides.sectionTitle: A Combine pipeline end to end
slides.markdown:
Combine models asynchronous event streams as **publishers** and **subscribers**, connected through a chain of **operators** that transform values along the way — conceptually the same idea as RxSwift or reactive streams elsewhere, native to Apple's platforms.

![Combine pipeline from a text field publisher through debounce, map, and filter to a sink](assets/combine-pipeline.svg)

assets.alt: Combine pipeline from a text field publisher through debounce, map, and filter to a sink

slides.subTitle: map, filter, debounce, combineLatest
slides.markdown:
A handful of operators cover most real usage:

- **map** — transform each value (a keystroke event into the current text).
- **filter** — drop values that don't matter (skip empty search strings).
- **debounce** — wait for a quiet period before emitting, collapsing rapid-fire events into one (search-as-you-type without firing on every keystroke).
- **combineLatest** — merge two publishers, emitting whenever *either* produces a new value, paired with the other's latest (validating a form once both a username and password publisher have emitted).

The reason these matter beyond convenience: they move filtering and timing logic **out of imperative callback code and into a declarative pipeline**, which is easier to reason about and test in isolation — you can unit-test a Combine pipeline by feeding it test values and asserting on the output, without spinning up any UI.

slides.subTitle: what changed vs ObservableObject
slides.markdown:
| | ObservableObject | @Observable (Observation) |
|---|---|---|
| Change tracking | whole-object — any @Published change fires objectWillChange | per-property — SwiftUI tracks exactly which properties a view actually reads |
| Over-render risk | high — a view reading one property re-renders on *any* published change | low — unread properties changing doesn't trigger a re-render |
| Boilerplate | @Published on every property | plain properties, one @Observable macro on the class |
| View-side wrapper | @StateObject / @ObservedObject | plain property, no wrapper needed for reading |

The practical win is fewer wasted re-renders: a view that only reads `cart.total` used to re-render whenever *any* `@Published` property on `CartViewModel` changed, even `items` it never looked at. `@Observable` tracks reads at the property level, so that view now only re-renders when `total` itself changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Combine vs async/await for a one-shot call
slides.markdown:
For a single network request with one response, `async`/`await` is almost always simpler than standing up a Combine pipeline — `let data = try await client.fetch()` reads linearly, with no publishers, subscribers, or cancellables to manage.

Combine earns its complexity for genuinely **stream-like** problems: a continuous sequence of values over time (search-as-you-type, a live price feed, merging multiple independent async sources with `combineLatest`), or when you need operators like `debounce`/`throttle` that don't have a clean `async`/`await` equivalent without hand-rolling them.

Many codebases now default to structured concurrency for one-shot work and reserve Combine specifically for multi-value streams — not a hard rule, but a good instinct for which tool actually fits the shape of the problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a leak from an unstored cancellable

slides.markdown:
Marking every single property `@Published` — including ones no view actually displays, like an internal retry counter or a cached intermediate value — means every mutation of that internal bookkeeping fires `objectWillChange` and triggers a re-render check on every view observing the object, even views that never read that property.

At small scale this is invisible. On a screen with several observed objects and rapid internal state churn (a live-updating counter, frequent cache writes), it becomes measurable jank — the view diffing machinery runs far more often than the visible output changes. The fix under `ObservableObject` is discipline: only `@Published` what a view actually renders, and keep purely internal state as plain, unpublished properties. Migrating to `@Observable` (Observation) removes this failure mode almost entirely, since it tracks property-level reads rather than firing on any change.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: pick the granularity that matches the read pattern
slides.markdown:
A junior answer treats state management as one binary choice — 'use ObservableObject.' A senior answer matches the tool to how state is actually **read**: a value read by exactly one view and never shared belongs in `@State`; a reference type read by several views at different granularities belongs behind `@Observable` so each view only re-renders for the slice it reads; a genuinely async, multi-value stream (search debouncing, a live feed, merging sources) is where Combine's operators still earn their place even after Observation's arrival.

The question worth asking before reaching for any of these: does this view actually need to re-render when this piece of data changes, or am I just defaulting to the pattern the rest of the codebase uses? Over-scoped observability is the most common source of SwiftUI performance complaints in production apps, and it's almost always fixable without a rewrite — just narrower reads and the right property wrapper.
